newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris couture season opens with eye on the matron.
newsitem.headline: Paris couture season opens with eye on the matron.

text.p: The Autumn-Winter haute couture season began in Paris on Sunday but the splash of the week was likely to come later when British designer Alexander McQueen unveils a collection reportedly containing human body parts.
McQueen, who has designed for Givenchy since October, has been accused by competitors of trying to recycle bits of human bone and blood in his new collection, according to the Sunday Times of London.
The report could not immediately be confirmed, and the collection will not be formally unveiled until Monday, at a Paris medical school.
But the controversial designer has been known to use human hair, blood and insects in catwalk presentations for his own label.
In the first shows of the new season, French fashion houses Nina Ricci and Torrente showed collections aiming for mature women who shun the less-is-more fashion ideal.

Rosette Mette-Torrente recycled the dandy look for Torrente, matching tweed riding coats with ascots and waistcoats over white poplin shirts, then threw political correctness to the wind by trimming wool coats with voluminous cuffs and collars of fox fur, mink or ostrich feathers.
Their linings sometimes matched the print of featherweight crepe dresses underneath.

Satin -- in splashy shocking pink and chartreuse or icy blue, pearl and silver -- was the fabric of choice for evening sheaths or dinner jackets, with sequins flashing from pockets and lapels and paired with matching trousers or long slit skirts.
Nodding to the Oriental trend that flourished on ready-to-wear catwalks in March, Mette-Torrente sent out floral kimono jackets on soft pyjama trousers for society hostesses at home.

Fashion houses often call on famous faces to appear on their catwalks to boost their visibility, and Torrente was no exception. Charlie Chaplin's grandaughter Dolores was the bride in spreading skirts and mink-edged jacket of ivory faille silk.

To fill out the ranks this season, the Chambre Syndicale, French fashion's governing body, has invited two young couturiers to show their collections: Adeline Andre, who unveils her designs on Monday, and Dominique Sirop, who will show on Tuesday.
The new additions bring to 22 the number of houses showing this season for an audience of some 900 journalists from 43 different countries, and a fast shrinking client base.
The Chambre Syndicale, which has every interest in promoting couture as a thriving industry, maintains that 2,000 women still buy the costly, one-of-a-kind haute couture creations.
But industry insiders estimate more realistically that there are only a few hundred clients left today in a world where few can pay the astronomical sums required to embody haute couture.
